RagShortTexts: Blade quality depends on material, heat treatment and workmanship.
Pattern welding, crucible steel and legends about river water are distinct explanations.

Variants.Content: Legend credited the mineral sands of the Tagus with giving Toledo swordsmiths their quenching skill, producing blades flexible enough to bend into arcs without snapping. Whatever the river contributed, the city's smiths were famous for tempering fine steel. In the Levant, Syrian artisans made crucible Wootz steel into the watered patterns known as Damascus blades, whose carbon structure in the metal gave the edge a hard cutting bite. These blades were traded across the Mediterranean and prized by knights and merchants alike. Whether the steel came from Iberia or the East, a well-made blade was worth a fortune, and buyers paid for proof of its temper before they paid for its hilt.

A smith judges a blade through material, heat treatment and workmanship rather than the fame of a river alone. Pattern welding and crucible steel can produce different visible structures and must not be confused. Toledo's reputation supports trade, but a story about water from the Tagus is not a technical account of carbon control or proof that every blade shares one process.

An authentic Toledo arming sword fetches the price of five warhorses in the bazaar. Cheap iron blades notch and warp against iron rims, but a well-tempered steel blade shears mail links and keeps its edge through many fights. Oil the blade after every wet march, check the fuller for cracks, and never use it to pry open a crate.
